Getting Started

How to Use This Planner

Welcome. This planner helps you plan your whole homestead for the year, from the garden to the animals to the pantry, and makes it easy to keep going once the season gets busy.

You can use it two ways. On its own, it's a complete paper planner, and every page works with a pencil and a few minutes. Alongside the Homestead Keeper app, it's the paper front end. You plan here, then the app keeps the record alive, updates itself, and reminds you what's due.

Why plan your homestead?
See the whole year

Know what's coming before the season gets busy.

Nothing slips

Sows, sprays, breedings, and reviews all in one place.

Plan once

Set it up in an afternoon, follow it all year.

Grows with you

Fine on its own, better with the app.

How it's organized

Plan it.

  • Start with the season. Set your frost dates and see the whole year at a glance, so everything lands at the right time for where you live.
  • Then work through the hubs. A page for each part of your homestead, in the same names the app uses.
  • Print the templates you need. Reusable pages like Individual Animal and Crop Planting are meant to be printed as many times as you like.

Dates work from your frost date, not the calendar. Nothing here requires the app, but the app makes it easier.

Reference

A Few Words We Use

The planner uses the same words as the Homestead Keeper app, so the two feel like one thing.

Homestead is your whole place, everything you manage.
Place is a named spot on your homestead, like the barn or the root cellar.
Specific Spot is a finer location within a Place, like a nest box wall or row three.
Growing Area is a place you grow food: a bed, a greenhouse, an herb garden.
Crop Planting is one crop you've put in, with its variety, dates, and notes.
Field Log is a quick note that something happened, like fed, pruned, or inspected.
Record is a saved log entry with the details (date, cost, notes).
Timeline is the story of one thing, newest first.
Reminder is a task that's due and comes back on a schedule.
Upcoming Work is what's due soon across a part of your homestead.
Current Status is the living state of something: Active, Sold, Retired.
Lifecycle events is the moments that change an animal's status: Acquired, Born, Weaned, Moved, Sold, Processed, Retired.

The hubs are just the parts of your homestead: Garden, Orchard, Animals, Bees, Property, Equipment, Inventory, Food & Pantry, Off-grid, Weather & Seasons, Wildlife & Pests, Forestry, and Emergency Prep.

The Season

The Homestead Year

This walks through the year by season instead of by month, because a homestead in Vermont and one in Georgia are on completely different clocks. Everything is written around your own frost dates, so it lands right wherever you are.

Early Spring roughly six to ten weeks before your last frost

The quiet, hopeful stretch. Start your slow crops indoors, like onions, peppers, and tomatoes. Dig out last year's seeds, see what's still good, and note what you're short on in Inventory. Get the dormant pruning finished in the Orchard and put down a dormant oil spray before the trees wake up. If you're growing the flock, order chicks and sketch out your spring breeding. Keep half an eye on the forecast for a late Frost Event.

Late Spring right around your last frost

Now it speeds up. Harden off and transplant, direct sow your warm weather crops, and get your first Crop Plantings in the ground. In the Orchard, spray at petal fall and plant any new Fruit Trees. This is baby season too, so you'll be logging births (Born), moving animals out to pasture (Moved), and staying ahead of parasites. Give the hives their first real spring inspection, and eat down last season's stores while you're at it.

Summer

Head down, hands busy. Keep sowing in succession, keep the water on, and start bringing in the first Harvest. Watch for trouble and write down any Pest Sighting or Deer Pressure. The preserving starts in earnest now, with canning, freezing, dehydrating, and fermenting. The animals hit their stride, so your Production climbs, and it's a good time to plan fall breeding.

The Homestead Keeper PlannerPlan it on paper. Keep it in the app.5
The Season

The Homestead Year continued

Late Summer

The big push. Preserve everything that's coming in, get your fall crops going, and save seed from your best plants. On the animal side you're weaning (Weaned) and making your keep or sell calls (Sold). The Orchard fruit comes in now, so weigh your yields. When the shelves fill up, count what you've actually put by (Items Stored).

Fall before your first frost

Time to batten down. Bring in the last harvest before that first Frost Event, put the Growing Areas to bed, and get your cover crops in. Breed for spring births and stock up on Feed before the price climbs. Cut, split, and stack your firewood, and walk the trails before the snow flies. Winterize your water lines, your generator, and your buildings, and test the Generator Plan.

Winter

Rest, plan, and fix. Look back at how the year went and lay out next season's Crop Plantings while it's fresh. Get the off season maintenance done on your equipment. Keep the animals warm and watered, and mind the due dates for anything bred to kid or lamb in spring. Do a deep Inventory count, and run through your storm readiness, including your Evacuation Note and contacts.

No hard frost where you live? Anchor to your wet and dry seasons or your local planting windows instead, and this same rhythm still works.

In the app: this same rhythm turns into dated Upcoming Work and gentle reminders, so you're not the one keeping the whole calendar in your head.

Hub

Bees

Hives, inspections, and honey harvests.

Beekeeping runs on a rhythm of regular inspections. This page is a reminder of the beats. The Hive template is where you log them.

Inspection rhythm
  • Spring: first inspection, check stores, add supers as they build.
  • Summer: watch for swarming, monitor mites, pull honey when it's capped.
  • Fall: feed as needed, treat for mites, wrap or shelter for winter.
  • Winter: leave them be, heft for stores, clear entrances after storms.
In the app: log each inspection on the hive and let the checks (Hive inspection, Feed check, Mite count) become Upcoming Work.
Template for this hub: Hive.
The Homestead Keeper PlannerPlan it on paper. Keep it in the app.16
Hub

Off-grid

Solar, water, power, and backup systems.

Off-grid systems are quiet until they aren't. A short maintenance rhythm keeps the lights on and the water running.

Maintenance rhythm
  • List your systems (solar array, batteries, well pump, generator, rain catchment).
  • Monthly: a quick check of each system and its readings.
  • Seasonally: service the generator, check battery levels, clean the panels, winterize the water.
In the app: track each system like any other asset, keep its service history, and let the monthly and annual checks turn into reminders.
Template for this hub: Equipment and Asset.
The Homestead Keeper PlannerPlan it on paper. Keep it in the app.17
Hub

Forestry

Woodlot, firewood, trails, and habitat.

The woodlot is a long game, but firewood is a yearly one, so most of this is about staying ahead of the cold.

Yearly rhythm
  • Cut, split, and stack firewood a season ahead so it's dry when you need it.
  • Walk and clear the trails before winter.
  • Note any tree work, invasive species, or habitat projects.
In the app: set up your Forestry Areas (Woodlot, Firewood Area, Trail, Habitat Project) and log the work with the Field Log so it lands on Upcoming Work.
No dedicated paper template yet. Use a blank note page or the app.
The Homestead Keeper PlannerPlan it on paper. Keep it in the app.18
Hub

Wildlife & Pests

Sightings, predator pressure, and habitat notes.

Keeping a simple record of what you're seeing helps you spot a pattern before it becomes a problem.

What to jot down
  • Pest Sightings (aphids, squash bugs, and the like) and where you saw them.
  • Predator Sightings and any losses.
  • Deer, rodent, and bird pressure through the season.
  • Habitat notes (hedgerows, pollinators, corridors).
In the app: log each one as a record under Wildlife & Pests so you can look back over the season and see the trend.
No dedicated paper template. A blank note page or the app works fine.
The Homestead Keeper PlannerPlan it on paper. Keep it in the app.19
Hub

Weather & Seasons

Frost dates, rainfall, and seasonal notes.

Your frost dates drive the whole planting year, so this page is mostly about writing them down and tracking what the weather actually does.

What to track
  • Your average last and first frost (see the Frost-Date and Season Worksheet).
  • Rainfall totals and dry spells.
  • Notable events: storms, a hard freeze, an early or late frost.
  • First and last frost as they actually happen, to sharpen next year's dates.
In the app: log observations as records under Weather & Seasons, and set your frost dates once so the app can schedule your plantings.
See also: the Frost-Date and Season Worksheet in the seasonal section.

The Next Step

Take It Further with Homestead Keeper

You've planned your year on paper. Homestead Keeper keeps it alive. Everything in this planner maps straight to the app, in the same words, so nothing feels new when you open it.

What the app does that paper can't
  • It schedules your garden for you. Set your frost dates once and every Crop Planting gets its windows worked out and dropped into Upcoming Work.
  • It remembers so you don't have to. Care, sprays, service, and reviews come back around as reminders.
  • It keeps each thing's whole story. Every animal, planting, and tool gets a Timeline, and an animal's Current Status updates itself.
  • It hands you clean records. Export an animal's full record, or a season's, as a tidy PDF for a buyer or your vet (with Pro).
  • It counts your shelves and bins. Inventory and Food & Pantry warn you before you run low or something expires.
Start your Homestead

Scan the code or visit homesteadkeeper.com. Plan it here, keep it there.
